topics.title: Diuretics
topics.class: Thiazides, loop diuretics, potassium-sparing diuretics
topics.moa: Thiazides inhibit the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Loop diuretics inhibit NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists reduce aldosterone-mediated sodium retention and potassium loss.
topics.uses: Hypertension, oedema, heart failure, and selected electrolyte or endocrine conditions depending on the agent.
topics.risks: Volume depletion, hypotension, kidney-function changes, and electrolyte abnormalities. Loop/thiazide agents may lower potassium; spironolactone/eplerenone may raise potassium. Thiazides can affect uric acid and glucose.
topics.interactions: NSAIDs can reduce diuretic and antihypertensive effects and worsen renal risk; combining potassium-raising medicines with potassium-sparing agents increases hyperkalaemia risk. Lithium concentrations may rise with some diuretics.
topics.counsel: Take at a practical time that limits nocturia; monitor blood pressure, weight when advised, kidney function and electrolytes. Seek advice for marked weakness, fainting, or significant dehydration.
learning_objectives: Explain the place of diuretics in pharmacy practice and identify the main medicine classes.
Connect the mechanism of action to the intended clinical effect and the most relevant adverse effects.
Recognise patient factors, interactions, monitoring needs and counselling points that change safe use.
topics.deep_explanation:
Diuretics — expanded study explanation.

1) Core concept and class: Thiazides, loop diuretics, potassium-sparing diuretics. Medicines within one class often share a broad mechanism, but they are not automatically interchangeable. Differences in selectivity, duration, formulation, route, metabolism, renal clearance and evidence for particular indications can change the preferred option.

2) Mechanism-to-effect reasoning: Thiazides inhibit the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Loop diuretics inhibit NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists reduce aldosterone-mediated sodium retention and potassium loss. When revising, follow the chain from target or physiological process → organ-level effect → expected benefit → predictable adverse effects. This helps explain why a medicine may help one condition while worsening another.

3) Clinical role: Hypertension, oedema, heart failure, and selected electrolyte or endocrine conditions depending on the agent. The indication should be confirmed before recommending treatment. Consider symptom severity, duration, previous treatment, age, pregnancy possibility where relevant, allergies, comorbidities, kidney/liver function, concurrent medicines and the need for referral. A medicine suitable for one patient may be inappropriate for another.

4) Safety interpretation: Volume depletion, hypotension, kidney-function changes, and electrolyte abnormalities. Loop/thiazide agents may lower potassium; spironolactone/eplerenone may raise potassium. Thiazides can affect uric acid and glucose. Distinguish common, usually manageable effects from serious warning symptoms. Review the product information for the exact active ingredient and formulation; do not assume all products in a broad class have identical risks. Do not stop long-term prescription therapy abruptly unless a clinician directs it, except where emergency advice is needed for a severe reaction.

Check whether the patient has a diagnosis or is self-treating an undiagnosed symptom. Review contraindications and relevant baseline measurements/laboratory tests for the exact drug. If information is missing or risk is high, refer rather than guessing.

Define a baseline where appropriate, the expected benefit, the time at which response should be reviewed, adverse effects to ask about, and objective measures if relevant. Take at a practical time that limits nocturia; monitor blood pressure, weight when advised, kidney function and electrolytes. Seek advice for marked weakness, fainting, or significant dehydration. Confirm who is responsible for follow-up and what the patient should do if treatment is ineffective or not tolerated. topics.interactions_deep: Interaction review: NSAIDs can reduce diuretic and antihypertensive effects and worsen renal risk; combining potassium-raising medicines with potassium-sparing agents increases hyperkalaemia risk. Consider additive pharmacodynamic effects (for example, bleeding, sedation, hypotension or electrolyte changes), and pharmacokinetic effects on absorption, metabolism or excretion. Rapid deterioration, severe or unusual symptoms, suspected serious adverse drug reaction, or signs of overdose: urgent assessment according to local emergency pathways.

Persistent/worsening symptoms, treatment failure, uncertain diagnosis, vulnerable patient, or important contraindication: refer to a qualified clinician/pharmacist rather than extending self-treatment.

topics.title: ACE inhibitors and ARBs
topics.class: ACE inhibitors (e.g., enalapril, lisinopril); ARBs (e.g., losartan, valsartan)
topics.moa: ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II formation and aldosterone release. ARBs block the angiotensin II AT₁ receptor. Both reduce vasoconstriction and aldosterone effects.
topics.uses: Hypertension, heart failure, and kidney protection in selected patients, particularly with albuminuria, depending on guideline and patient factors.
topics.risks: Hypotension, increased potassium, and a rise in creatinine can occur. ACE inhibitors may cause cough and rarely angioedema. Avoid during pregnancy; assess renal artery stenosis and kidney function context.
topics.interactions: Avoid routine ACE inhibitor + ARB combination. Potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics and some other drugs raise hyperkalaemia risk; NSAIDs can worsen renal function.
topics.counsel: Check blood pressure, creatinine/eGFR and potassium at baseline and after initiation or dose changes as directed. Facial, lip or tongue swelling needs emergency care.

topics.title: Beta blockers
topics.class: Examples: bisoprolol, metoprolol, carvedilol, propranolol
topics.moa: Block beta-adrenergic receptors, reducing heart rate and contractility; selected agents also reduce renin release. Receptor selectivity and additional alpha-blockade vary by agent.
topics.uses: Selected patients with heart failure, angina, rate control, post-myocardial infarction care, hypertension, migraine prevention or tremor depending on the agent.
topics.risks: Bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, sexual adverse effects; may mask some hypoglycaemia warning symptoms. Non-selective agents can provoke bronchospasm in susceptible patients.
topics.interactions: Other rate-slowing drugs (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) can increase bradycardia/heart block risk. Abrupt withdrawal can worsen angina or trigger events.
topics.counsel: Do not stop suddenly without clinical advice. Monitor pulse and blood pressure as instructed; report fainting, severe wheeze or unusually slow pulse.
learning_objectives: Explain the place of beta blockers in pharmacy practice and identify the main medicine classes.
Connect the mechanism of action to the intended clinical effect and the most relevant adverse effects.

topics.title: Antiplatelets and anticoagulants
topics.class: Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors, heparins, warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants
topics.moa: Antiplatelets reduce platelet activation/aggregation. Anticoagulants inhibit clotting factors or their synthesis, reducing fibrin-clot formation; mechanisms differ by medicine.
topics.uses: Prevention/treatment of arterial or venous thrombosis according to diagnosis, procedure and risk assessment.
topics.risks: Bleeding is the key class concern. Agent-specific issues include gastrointestinal injury with aspirin, thrombocytopenia with heparins, and drug/renal-function constraints with several oral anticoagulants.
topics.interactions: NSAIDs and other antithrombotics can increase bleeding. Warfarin has many drug/food interactions and requires INR monitoring. Strong enzyme/P-gp modifiers may alter some direct oral anticoagulants.
topics.counsel: Follow the exact prescribed schedule; never double missed doses without medicine-specific instructions. Seek urgent help for serious bleeding, black stools, blood in urine, severe headache after injury, or unexplained major bruising.
learning_objectives: Explain the place of antiplatelets and anticoagulants in pharmacy practice and identify the main medicine classes.

topics.title: Calcium-channel blockers
topics.class: Dihydropyridines and non-dihydropyridines
topics.moa: Dihydropyridines predominantly relax vascular smooth muscle; verapamil and diltiazem also slow AV-node conduction and reduce heart rate.
topics.uses: Hypertension and angina; selected agents for rate control or arrhythmias when clinically appropriate.
topics.risks: Ankle oedema, flushing, headache and dizziness; verapamil may cause constipation and bradycardia. Avoid assuming all agents have the same cardiac effects.
topics.interactions: CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers may alter exposure; verapamil/diltiazem can interact with beta blockers and other rate-slowing medicines. Grapefruit effects are product-specific.
topics.counsel: Take consistently as directed; do not crush modified-release formulations unless product instructions allow it. Report fainting, marked slow pulse or troublesome swelling.
learning_objectives: Explain the clinical role and safety priorities for calcium-channel blockers.

topics.title: Statins and lipid-lowering therapy
topics.class: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors and other lipid-lowering medicines
topics.moa: Statins inhibit hepatic cholesterol synthesis and increase LDL-receptor-mediated clearance. Other agents act through different pathways and may be added based on risk and response.

topics.counsel: Explain long-term risk reduction even when the patient feels well. Report unexplained severe muscle pain or weakness, especially with systemic illness or dark urine.

topics.uses: Inhaled medicines for asthma/COPD when prescribed and appropriate for the patient.
topics.risks: Poor technique reduces dose reaching the lungs; poor cleaning or failure to use prescribed spacer may affect delivery.

topics.deep_explanation:
Metered-dose inhaler and spacer — expanded study explanation.

1) Core concept and class: Respiratory drug delivery devices. Medicines within one class often share a broad mechanism, but they are not automatically interchangeable. Differences in selectivity, duration, formulation, route, metabolism, renal clearance and evidence for particular indications can change the preferred option.

2) Mechanism-to-effect reasoning: The device aerosolises medicine; a spacer holds the aerosol briefly and can improve delivery/coordination. When revising, follow the chain from target or physiological process → organ-level effect → expected benefit → predictable adverse effects. This helps explain why a medicine may help one condition while worsening another.

3) Clinical role: Inhaled medicines for asthma/COPD when prescribed and appropriate for the patient. The indication should be confirmed before recommending treatment. Consider symptom severity, duration, previous treatment, age, pregnancy possibility where relevant, allergies, comorbidities, kidney/liver function, concurrent medicines and the need for referral. A medicine suitable for one patient may be inappropriate for another.

4) Safety interpretation: Poor technique reduces dose reaching the lungs; poor cleaning or failure to use prescribed spacer may affect delivery. Distinguish common, usually manageable effects from serious warning symptoms. Review the product information for the exact active ingredient and formulation; do not assume all products in a broad class have identical risks. Do not stop long-term prescription therapy abruptly unless a clinician directs it, except where emergency advice is needed for a severe reaction.
topics.clinical_assessment: Before counselling or supporting a treatment decision, clarify the presenting problem, onset and duration, severity, relevant history, allergies, current prescription/OTC/herbal products, prior response and adherence. Check whether the patient has a diagnosis or is self-treating an undiagnosed symptom. Review contraindications and relevant baseline measurements/laboratory tests for the exact drug. If information is missing or risk is high, refer rather than guessing.
topics.monitoring_and_follow_up: Monitoring should match the drug and indication, not just the class name. Define a baseline where appropriate, the expected benefit, the time at which response should be reviewed, adverse effects to ask about, and objective measures if relevant. Remove cap and check mouthpiece; shake if instructed; breathe out; seal lips; press once while inhaling slowly and deeply, then hold breath if able. With a spacer, follow device instructions and inhale promptly or take the recommended tidal breaths. Rinse mouth after inhaled corticosteroids. Confirm who is responsible for follow-up and what the patient should do if treatment is ineffective or not tolerated. Never invent a monitoring interval: use the current local guideline, product information and prescriber plan.
topics.interactions_deep: Interaction review: Device technique is not a pharmacological interaction, but correct device choice affects delivered dose. In addition, reconcile all medicines including non-prescription products, supplements and recently stopped drugs. Consider additive pharmacodynamic effects (for example, bleeding, sedation, hypotension or electrolyte changes), and pharmacokinetic effects on absorption, metabolism or excretion. A potential interaction does not always mean a combination is forbidden; assess clinical significance and consult a reliable interaction checker/formulary when uncertain.
patient_counselling_checklist: Explain the purpose in plain language and what improvement to expect; avoid promising a cure or immediate effect when that is not expected.
Demonstrate the correct route and technique for the actual dosage form, and ask the patient to repeat the key steps.
Explain missed-dose advice using the product-specific instructions; do not advise doubling doses unless the official instructions explicitly say so.
Discuss important adverse effects, the action to take if they occur, storage, expiry and safe disposal.
Use teach-back: ask the patient to describe how and when they will use the medicine and when they will seek help.
red_flags: Suspected severe allergic reaction, breathing difficulty, collapse, or swelling of the face/tongue: urgent emergency assessment.
Rapid deterioration, severe or unusual symptoms, suspected serious adverse drug reaction, or signs of overdose: urgent assessment according to local emergency pathways.

Persistent/worsening symptoms, treatment failure, uncertain diagnosis, vulnerable patient, or important contraindication: refer to a qualified clinician/pharmacist rather than extending self-treatment.
exam_pearls: Do not memorise Metered-dose inhaler and spacer as a list alone: link each mechanism to both benefit and toxicity.
A safe answer includes indication, patient-specific risk, interaction review, counselling, monitoring and referral—not only the drug name.
Distinguish class effects from agent-specific effects and formulation-specific administration instructions.
